spots.desc: Busan's modern century — colonial port, wartime capital, boom town — told inside the former Bank of Korea branch, fully opened in 2024, with an annex in a 1929 colonial-era building nearby.
spots.tip: Free, closed Mondays. Start here: it frames everything else on the walk, and the 40 Steps are minutes away.
spots.mapQ: Busan Modern and Contemporary History Museum

spots.name: Former Government Building (Seokdang Museum)
spots.desc: The red-brick 1925 Gyeongnam Provincial Hall housed the national government through the wartime years; today it is Dong-A University's Seokdang Museum and a registered cultural heritage building.
spots.tip: Five minutes uphill from the Memorial Hall. Look for the restored Busan streetcar displayed outside — the city's last tram.

spots.name: UN Peace Memorial Hall
spots.desc: A modern exhibition hall on the UN's part in the war — veteran testimonies, uniforms, the Busan Perimeter explained — anchoring the Peace Park zone beside the cemetery.
spots.tip: Free; visit after the cemetery via leafy UN Peace Park. A good indoor fallback when it rains.

spots.name: Busan Citizens Park
spots.desc: The US Army's Camp Hialeah until 2006, reborn as the city's great lawn in 2014 — preserved base buildings and a small history hall keep the military-era layers visible.
spots.tip: A gentle decompression stop after the heavy sites — kids can run, and the history hall is free.

faq: Why is Busan called Korea's wartime capital?

When Seoul fell in June 1950 the government retreated south, and from August 1950 (with one brief return north) until August 1953 Busan was the seat of the Republic of Korea — 1,023 days in all. The Busan Perimeter along the Nakdong River held, so it was the only major city never captured.
Is the UN Memorial Cemetery free, and how do I get there?

Yes, entry is free. Take Metro Line 2 to Daeyeon Station, Exit 3, then walk about 15 minutes; buses and taxis also work. Typical hours run roughly 09:00–17:00, later in summer — check the official UNMCK site before you go, especially around ceremony dates.
What etiquette should I follow at the cemetery?

Keep voices low, dress neatly, and stay on the paths — grave plots and lawns are off-limits. No food, drinks or pets inside. Photography is allowed, but be discreet near mourners and during ceremonies. Treat it as you would any national cemetery: you are a guest of eleven nations' families.
How much time does the war-history route take?

Half a day covers the downtown sites — the history museum, 40 Steps and Memorial Hall. A full day adds the UN Memorial Cemetery, Peace Memorial Hall and Busan Museum without rushing. With only two hours, choose the cemetery; it is the emotional core of the whole story.
What is 'Turn Toward Busan'?

Every 11 November at 11:00, sirens sound and participants worldwide — veterans, families, schoolchildren — face Busan for a minute of silence honoring the UN fallen buried here. Memorial events run at the cemetery that week; check the official UNMCK page for each year's programme.
Is this route okay with children?

Yes — Korean school groups visit constantly. The 40 Steps street and Busan Citizens Park are easy wins, and the museums are free. Brief children on cemetery quiet rules before the gates; if energy runs low, our busan-with-kids guide has nearby escapes.
How do Gamcheon and Gukje Market connect to the war?

Directly. Gamcheon's terraced lanes grew from 1950s refugee and Taegeukdo settlements, and Gukje Market rose on relief goods and surplus traded by displaced people. This page gives you the history; the hidden-neighborhoods and markets-street-food guides walk you through the places themselves.
tips: Every core site on this page is free — cemetery, both museums, Memorial Hall, 40 Steps. Budget only transport and lunch.
Metro shorthand: Jungang (Line 1) for the 40 Steps, Toseong (Line 1) for the Memorial Hall, Daeyeon (Line 2) for the cemetery.
Most museums on this route close Mondays; the cemetery and the 40 Steps street stay open every day.
The cemetery closes by early evening, earlier in winter — never leave it for last on a short winter day.
Eat milmyeon for lunch — it is wartime refugee food itself; the eat-like-a-local guide has the full story.
Rain plan: both history museums and the UN Peace Memorial Hall are fully indoors — the rainy-day guide has more.
Visiting around 11 November? Ceremonies peak that week — deeply moving, but check the official UNMCK page for timings and access changes.
Brief kids on cemetery quiet before the gates, and promise them Busan Citizens Park's lawns afterward.

en.h1: Busan on a Budget — What a Day Really Costs
en.title: Busan on a Budget: What a Day Really Costs | KoreaPlus
en.metaDesc: What a Busan day really costs: three honest daily budgets in won, the free list, ₩6,000 day-pass math, market eating and the overspends locals skip.
en.lead: Busan is one of Korea's kindest big cities to a wallet — the best things here are genuinely free and the best food is the cheapest. Here's what a real day costs at three honest levels, the metro math, and the markups we locals quietly walk past. All prices are typical ranges; check official pages for anything dated.
facts: Metro ride: about ₩1,600 by card · 1-day pass ₩6,000 (metro only)
Taxi base fare ₩4,800 · night surcharge 23:00–04:00
Beomeosa and 64 other temples: admission fees abolished May 2023
Gwangalli M Drone Light Show: free, Saturdays, twice a night
Gukbap staple meal: typically ₩8,000–10,000 · franchise coffee about ₩2,000
Tipping does not exist in Korea — prices are final

sections.h: Three honest daily budgets
paras: These are full-day figures — bed, three meals, transport, one paid activity — at typical 2026 prices, per person. Busan rewards the low end: an ₩8,000–10,000 gukbap (국밥) outclasses most ₩30,000 tourist dinners. Your pillow moves the number more than anything else, so the tiers differ mainly by where you sleep and one daily splurge.
list: Backpacker, roughly ₩50,000–70,000: guesthouse dorm (₩20,000–35,000), gukbap and market meals, ₩2,000 franchise coffee, ₩6,000 metro day pass, free beaches and temples.
Mid-range, roughly ₩90,000–140,000: clean motel or business hotel (₩50,000–80,000), one proper sit-down meal, a jjimjilbang session (₩10,000–15,000), transit plus one short taxi.
Comfortable, roughly ₩180,000–300,000: 3–4-star hotel (₩120,000–200,000+, sea view extra), a hoe (회, raw fish) dinner, Spa Land at about ₩20,000, taxis whenever tired.

sections.h: The free list is the good list
paras: Busan's headline sights cost nothing: every beach, the Igidae (이기대) and Dalmaji coastal paths, Gamcheon's painted lanes, and — since Korea abolished temple admission fees in May 2023 — the grounds of Beomeosa (범어사) and 64 other Jogye temples. Saturdays add a free drone show over Gwangalli (광안리). Our beaches, night-views and temples guides map the details; a backpacker day can be built entirely from this list.

sections.h: Transit math: pass, card or taxi
paras: A card ride on the metro is about ₩1,600 (₩1,700 by paper ticket or QR), so the ₩6,000 one-day pass breaks even on ride four — normal for a sightseeing day — and a ₩13,000 three-day version exists. For three or four people hopping a couple of stops, one taxi from the ₩4,800 base fare often beats everyone tapping separately. Fares rose twice recently, so treat these as typical and check current prices.

sections.h: Eat where the regulars eat
paras: The cheap food here is the good food. Follow office workers at lunch to dwaeji-gukbap (돼지국밥) or milmyeon (밀면) counters, where ₩8,000–10,000 buys a full meal with refillable sides and free water. Markets stack the snacks — eomuk (어묵), ssiat hotteok (씨앗호떡), tteokbokki — at roughly ₩1,000–3,000 apiece. Our eat-like-a-local and markets guides name names; the budget rule is simple: no photo menus, no touts, follow the queue.

sections.h: Sleep cheap by sleeping smart
paras: Your bed sets the budget. The same comfort costs least around Seomyeon (서면) and Nampo (남포동) — dorms typically ₩20,000–35,000, decent motels ₩50,000–80,000 — and most beside the Haeundae sand, where a sea view can nearly double a room. Sleeping central and metro-ing to the beaches is the local-approved cheat; our where-to-stay guide breaks down each area's price logic, and Friday–Saturday nights spike everywhere.

sections.h: Where tourists overspend — and locals don't
paras: The classic leaks: ₩7,000 lattes bought for a sea view the sand gives you free; hotel breakfasts at ₩20,000-plus when the gukbap house next door charges ₩9,000; taxis at rush hour, when the meter ticks while you crawl; and raw-fish dinners ordered without agreeing prices first. None are scams — they're just the tourist path of least resistance.

And the happiest saving of all: tipping does not exist in Korea. Not in taxis, restaurants, cafés or hotels — prices are final, service is included, and leaving extra genuinely confuses people. Budget exactly what the menu says.

spots.name: Gukje Market
spots.desc: Nampo's post-war market sprawl is budget headquarters: clothes, homewares and food alleys where ₩10,000 is a feast. It blends straight into Bupyeong Kkangtong Market (부평깡통시장) and the street-food rows.
spots.tip: Eat in the interior food alleys where the stallholders themselves lunch, not the outward tourist-facing rows — same dishes, calmer prices.

spots.name: Jagalchi Market
spots.desc: Korea's largest fish market. Raw fish is the splurge; the budget move is a grilled-fish set meal or eomuk from the stalls ringing the building, around ₩10,000.
spots.tip: Ordering hoe upstairs? Agree the all-in price — fish plus table-setting charge — before you sit down.

spots.name: Gamcheon Culture Village
spots.desc: The painted hillside costs nothing to wander — the best free half-day in the city. The optional ₩2,000 stamp map funds village projects and ends in souvenir postcards.
spots.tip: Take bus 2-2 from near Toseong Station uphill and walk down — spend energy, not money, in the lanes.

spots.name: Beomeosa
spots.desc: Busan's grandest temple dropped its admission fee in May 2023, when Korea scrapped charges at 65 Jogye-order temples. A genuine mountain monastery, now completely free to enter.
spots.tip: Metro to Beomeosa Station, then bus 90 up the mountain — the transit taps are the morning's entire cost.

spots.name: Gwangalli Beach
spots.desc: Gwangan Bridge views all evening for free, plus the M Drone Light Show on Saturday nights — currently twice a night, times shifting by season. Weather cancels at short notice.
spots.tip: Check the official show page that week, claim sand early — and remember nearby Millak Waterside Park is alcohol-free now.

spots.name: Igidae Coastal Walk
spots.desc: A free clifftop boardwalk with the city's best Gwangan Bridge panorama. Anywhere else, this two-hour coastal walk would sell tickets.
spots.tip: Start late afternoon and walk toward Oryukdo — sunset plus the bridge lights for a single bus fare.

spots.name: Dadaepo Beach
spots.desc: The end-of-Line-1 beach with Busan's widest sunset, entirely free. The Sunset Fountain of Dreams adds free evening shows in the warmer months — check the current schedule first.
spots.tip: It's a long ride out — this is the day the ₩6,000 metro pass earns its keep.

spots.name: Yongdusan Park
spots.desc: The free hilltop park above Nampo, reached by street escalators from the shopping alleys. Harbour views cost nothing; only the tower observatory charges.
spots.tip: Skip the paid tower — our night-views guide lists better panoramas that cost nothing at all.

faq: How much is a realistic daily budget for Busan?

Typically ₩50,000–70,000 for a dorm-and-markets backpacker day, ₩90,000–140,000 for a motel-and-restaurants middle, and ₩180,000–300,000 with a 3–4-star hotel and a raw-fish dinner. Weekday off-season trips land near the bottom of each band; summer weekends push the top. All figures are typical ranges, not quotes.
Is the ₩6,000 metro day pass worth it?

From the fourth ride, yes — card rides are about ₩1,600. But the pass covers the metro only; Gamcheon and Songdo need buses, where a T-money card with its free transfers within 30 minutes wins. Do the math against your actual route, not the brochure.
Do I need to tip anywhere in Busan?

No — nowhere, ever. Not taxis, restaurants, cafés or hotels. Prices are final and service is included; staff will chase you down the street to return money they think you forgot. Enjoy budgeting to the exact won printed on the menu.
Is Busan cheaper than Seoul?

Modestly, yes. Beds and market meals run a little lower, and far more of the headline sights are free — beaches, coastal walks, the Saturday drone show, temple grounds. The exception is high season in Haeundae, where sea-view rooms price like Seoul's smartest districts. Book those early or sleep inland.
When does a taxi beat the metro?

With three or four people going a stop or two, with luggage, or after the metro closes for the night. Base fare is ₩4,800. Avoid weekday rush hours around 8–9:30am and 6–7:30pm, when the meter ticks in stalled traffic, and note the 23:00–04:00 night surcharge.
How much cash should I carry?

Less than you'd think — cards work almost everywhere, taxis included. Keep ₩30,000–50,000 in small notes for market stalls, some old-school counters, and bus fares if you skip a transit card. ATMs marked 'Global' take foreign cards; airport exchange desks give the worst rates.
tips: A convenience-store breakfast — coffee, gimbap, fruit — runs about ₩4,000–5,000, and locals genuinely do it.
Budget coffee chains charge roughly ₩1,500–2,500 for an Americano; sea-view cafés charge ₩6,000–8,000 for the glass wall.
The day pass covers metro only — buses need T-money, which also gives free transfers within 30 minutes.
Restaurant water and side-dish refills are free; asking for more banchan is normal, not cheeky.
A jjimjilbang overnight (typically ₩15,000–25,000) is the classic budget bed — see our hot-springs guide.
Friday and Saturday nights spike room prices; shift beach-area stays to weekdays and pocket the difference.
Skip the ₩20,000-plus hotel breakfast — there's always a gukbap house within two blocks doing it better.
Millak Waterside Park has been alcohol-free since July 2023, with a ₩50,000 fine — older blogs still show the parties.

en.h1: Active Busan: Surf, Hike, Paddle, Run
en.title: Active Busan: Surf, Hike, Paddle & Run | KoreaPlus
en.metaDesc: Surf year-round at Songjeong, SUP under Gwangan Bridge, hike the Galmaetgil and Geumjeongsan ridge — a Busan local's guide to doing, not just seeing.
en.lead: Busan's coastline isn't just scenery — it's equipment. This is for travellers who'd rather stand on a board than at a viewpoint: Songjeong's year-round surf, SUP beneath Gwangan Bridge, the Galmaetgil's finest cliff section, Geumjeongsan's ridge, and the flat river paths locals run and ride at dawn. All doable without a car.
facts: The Galmaetgil totals about 278 km — '700 ri' — in 9 courses and 21 sections circling the entire city.
Songjeong is Korea's original year-round surf beach; schools rent boards and wetsuits every month of the year.
The Oryukdo Skywalk is free — a glass horseshoe hanging some 35 m above the sea.
Geumjeongsan's Joseon-era fortress wall runs roughly 18 km along the ridge, Korea's largest mountain fortress.
Lifeguarded sea swimming runs only from late June to mid-September; surfing and hiking never stop.

sections.h: Songjeong, Korea's year-round surf town
paras: One tunnel past Haeundae, Songjeong (송정) runs on surf time. A strip of schools along the beach road rents boards and wetsuits twelve months a year, and the sandy-bottomed beginner waves are as forgiving as Korea gets. A two-hour group lesson with all gear typically costs ₩50,000–70,000; book a day ahead in July–August. Autumn brings the cleanest swell, and locals keep paddling out right through January.
During the official swim season — roughly late June to mid-September — lifeguards split the water into swim and surf zones. Follow the flags and the surf-school staff and you'll be fine.

sections.h: SUP beneath the Gwangan Bridge
paras: Gwangalli (광안리) is the paddle shot everyone wants: you, a board, and Gwangan Bridge (광안대교) filling the frame. A designated SUP zone, set up in 2020, keeps paddlers clear of swimmers, and several shops on the strip run intro lessons and rentals with showers and lockers. Mornings are glassy; afternoons chop up. The sunset slot is the one to book — the bridge lights switch on while you're still afloat.

sections.h: The Galmaetgil — and the one section to do
paras: The Galmaetgil (갈맷길), 'seagull way' after the city's mascot bird, is Busan's 700-ri walking network — about 278 km in 9 courses and 21 sections looping the whole city. Nobody walks it all on holiday. The section worth flying for is the Oryukdo–Igidae coastal stretch: roughly 5 km of cliffs, boardwalks and skyline-across-the-water views.

Do it properly: bus 24 or 131 to Oryukdo (오륙도), the free glass Skywalk first, then north along the Igidae (이기대) cliffs to the Dongsaengmal trailhead — 2 to 2.5 hours with plenty of stairs. Use the toilets at either end and carry water; there is nothing in between. Our beaches guide covers the gentler shoreline strolls.

sections.h: Geumjeongsan: the ridge walk
paras: Geumjeongsan (금정산) is Busan's roof, and the Joseon-era fortress wall riding its ridge — around 18 km of it — is the city's classic hill day. The insider version: take the Geumgang Park cable car up from the Oncheonjang side, walk the ridge north to the fortress's North Gate, then drop to Beomeosa (범어사) and its metro station. Half a day, moderate legs. The temple itself belongs to our temples-and-mountains guide.

sections.h: Run and ride like a resident
paras: Dawn on Gwangalli sand is Busan's unofficial running club: firm low-tide sand, empty boardwalk, sunrise beside the bridge. Inland, the Oncheoncheon (온천천) stream path gives kilometres of flat, traffic-free tarmac through Dongnae — outrageous under April's cherry blossoms — and joins the Suyeong River path toward the sea.

Cyclists get the Nakdong estuary: pancake-flat levee paths where Korea's cross-country river trail ends. Public rental spots at Samnak (삼락) Ecological Park and on Eulsukdo (을숙도) island lend adult and kids' bikes — bring ID; hours are roughly 9 to 6, shorter in winter. Spin south to Dadaepo (다대포) for sunset.

sections.h: Seasons, safety, small print
paras: Winter reality: surfing continues in 5-mm rubber, boots and gloves (schools rent everything); SUP mostly hibernates November–March; hiking is at its crisp, clear best. Swimming belongs strictly to the lifeguarded season.

Respect the flags: rip currents do occur, so stay inside guarded zones. Jellyfish advisories peak in August — nets go up at the big beaches, and stings get rinsed with seawater, never fresh. Mountain trails can close for fire-prevention periods in spring and late autumn; check trailhead notices. And Dadaepo's Sunset Fountain of Dreams runs seasonally, roughly late April to October, resting Mondays — always check the official schedule.

spots.name: Songjeong Beach
spots.desc: Korea's surf-town original: soft sandy-bottom peaks, a beach road lined with surf schools, and a slower village rhythm one tunnel from Haeundae. Rentals and lessons run all twelve months.
spots.tip: Autumn has the year's cleanest swell; in July–August book a day ahead and stick to the flagged surf zone.

spots.name: Gwangalli Beach
spots.desc: Busan's SUP mecca since the paddle zone was designated in 2020 — glide with Gwangan Bridge filling the horizon, then join the dawn runners on the firm morning sand.
spots.tip: Book the sunset SUP slot for the bridge lights; calm mornings are easiest for first-timers.

spots.name: Oryukdo Skywalk
spots.desc: A free glass horseshoe jutting 35 m above the cliffs, eye-to-eye with the five-or-six islets that name it. The Galmaetgil's finest stretch starts right here.
spots.tip: Buses 24 and 131 stop nearby; it may close in strong wind, so pair it with the coastal hike either way.

spots.name: Igidae Coastal Park
spots.desc: Clifftop park carrying the Galmaetgil north from Oryukdo: boardwalks, rock shelves and the full Gwangan Bridge–skyline panorama across the water.
spots.tip: No shops or toilets mid-trail — carry water and wear proper shoes; the stairs are endless.

spots.name: Geumjeongsan
spots.desc: Busan's highest ridge, crowned by an 18-km Joseon fortress wall. Cable car up, ridge walk to the North Gate, temple descent — the definitive half-day hill.
spots.tip: The Geumgang Park cable car skips the sweaty ascent, but check its operating hours before you build the hike around it.

spots.name: Oncheoncheon Stream Path
spots.desc: The city's stream-side running artery: flat, lit, traffic-free tarmac and cycle path threading Dongnae's neighbourhoods, riotous with cherry blossoms each April.
spots.tip: Follow it downstream onto the Suyeong River path and you can run nearly to the sea.

spots.name: Dadaepo Beach
spots.desc: A vast, shallow sweep where the Nakdong River meets the sea — Busan's best sunset walk, with tidal flats and the seasonal Sunset Fountain of Dreams show.
spots.tip: The fountain runs roughly late April–October and rests Mondays — check the official schedule before making the trip.
spots.mapQ: Dadaepo Beach Sunset Fountain of Dreams

spots.name: Eulsukdo
spots.desc: Reed-covered estuary island and migratory-bird haven at the Nakdong's mouth, the hub of the delta's dead-flat cycle paths.
spots.tip: Public bike rental on the island and at nearby Samnak — bring ID; winter mornings bring the big bird flocks.
spots.mapQ: Eulsukdo Ecological Park bike rental Busan

faq: Can a total beginner really surf at Songjeong?

Yes — beginners are Songjeong's core business. Two-hour group lessons, typically ₩50,000–70,000 including board and wetsuit, run on soft sandy-bottom waves, and most people stand up on day one. Reserve a day ahead in summer; autumn is quieter with better waves.
I only have half a day — which Galmaetgil section should I walk?

The Oryukdo–Igidae coastal stretch: about 5 km and 2–2.5 hours of cliffs, boardwalks and skyline views. Take bus 24 or 131 to Oryukdo, do the free Skywalk, then walk north to Dongsaengmal. Carry water — nothing is sold en route.
Is anything doable in winter?

Plenty. Surfing runs all winter in thick rented wetsuits, hiking is at its clearest, and the flat cycle paths stay open. SUP mostly pauses November–March, and sea swimming waits for the lifeguarded season. Pack windproof layers — the sea wind bites.
Where do I rent a bicycle for the river paths?

Public rental spots operate at Samnak Ecological Park and on Eulsukdo, with adult and children's bikes — bring ID. Hours are roughly 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., shorter in winter. The estuary levee paths are flat enough for any fitness level.
How safe is the sea for swimming and paddling?

Swim only in lifeguarded zones during the official season, roughly late June to mid-September, and obey the flags — rip currents happen. Jellyfish advisories peak in late summer, when major beaches install protective nets. SUP operators provide flotation and keep paddlers inside the designated zone.
Do I need to book SUP at Gwangalli in advance?

Weekday walk-ins usually work, but sunset slots and summer weekends sell out — book those ahead. Sessions typically include a short intro, all equipment, and showers afterwards. Calm mornings are easiest for first-timers; afternoons get choppy.
